report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister’s claim is supported by the best direct trial evidence, though the effect is not absolute and results from smaller studies have been less precise.

The key study was a multicenter randomized trial (1,147 women) directly comparing chlorhexidine–alcohol with iodine–alcohol before cesarean delivery. Surgical-site infection within 30 days occurred in **4.0%** (23/572) with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus **7.3%** (42/575) with iodine–alcohol: relative risk **0.55** (95% CI 0.34–0.90). That is an absolute reduction of 3.3 percentage points—roughly one fewer infection per 30 preparations.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26844840/

A systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials likewise concluded that chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces cesarean SSI compared with povidone-iodine preparations.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/

**Important nuance:** not every individual trial finds a statistically significant difference. For example, a 311-participant pilot RCT favored chlorhexidine–alcohol numerically but was too small to establish a reliable difference.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34404473/

This is consistent with guidance recommending alcohol-based chlorhexidine for skin preparation before either elective or emergency cesarean section. The comparison is specifically about *skin* preparation; alcohol-based products should not be used for vaginal preparation because of mucosal irritation concerns.  
https://www.alignmnh.org/new-guidance-updated-who-recommendations-on-prevention-and-treatment-of-maternal-peripartum-infections/
